title: Shared-KV Slab Fragmenter for Low-Jitter Streaming Batch Formation
creator: Maya Patel
description: Goal: Reduce latency jitter and GPU memory pressure for long-running streaming chat sessions by improving batch formation heuristics that are KV-cache aware and memory-reservable. Background: Our current streaming batcher aggressively coalesces turns into microbatches based on time windows and token counts, which increases throughput but produces large P95 latency spikes when KV cache growth forces slab relocations or causes memory oversubscription on multi-tenant GPUs. This ticket designs and implements a slab-fragmenter approach that fragments batch boundaries to better align with KV hotsets and GPU slab reservations while preserving request-level latency SLOs for interactive chat.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New batcher variant (slab-fragmenter) deployed behind a feature flag for streaming chat routes. 2) P50 latency remains unchanged; P95 latency improves by at least 15% for workloads with >1.5k average KV entries per session. 3) GPU memory OOM events for streaming workloads reduced to zero in canary. 4) End-to-end correctness: token ordering and streaming semantics preserved, no response duplication. 5) Documentation + perf dashboard for the feature.
technical_design: Key ideas: (a) Shard-aware microbatching: classify incoming streaming turns by their KV-profile fingerprint (prefix reuse ratio, length delta) and form tentative microbatches that prefer grouping requests that reuse KV prefixes to maximize KV cache hits. (b) Slab reservation window: allocate a small per-batch GPU slab budget derived from session TTL and observed KV growth; if predicted per-batch slab exceed threshold, split the batch at safe token boundaries (turn boundaries or sentence boundaries) to avoid triggering kernel-level reallocation. (c) Fragmenter heuristic: when a candidate batch contains heterogeneous KV footprints, split into 'fragments' such that each fragment's estimated KV working set fits within slab reservation; allow ordered streaming across fragments with incremental KV attach/detach. (d) KV hot-slot pinning: detect top-K hot KV keys (across active sessions) and pin them to a reserved fast-slab region to reduce eviction churn. (e) Graceful spill policy: on memory pressure, drop non-critical prefetched prefixes and prioritize completion-facing prefixes. Trade-offs: additional CPU scheduling and fingerprinting cost; modest increase in scheduling complexity for better P95 and fewer OOMs. Safety: maintain single-request ordering and ensure fragments do not change content ordering or cause double-streaming of tokens.
implementation_notes: Phase 1: Instrument fingerprint extractor and estimated-kv-size model (spike done). Phase 2: Implement fragmenter in batcher codepath with feature flag (WIP). Phase 3: Canary on dedicated pool with synthetic load and a subset of production traffic. Phase 4: Rollout and rollback playbook. Data collection: per-batch KV hit ratio, slab-reservation vs actual memory, per-session KV growth curves, P50/P95/P99 latency for streaming completions.
experiments_and_results: Spike results (2026-02-24): ran 24h A/B test with 10% of streaming traffic routed to a prototype fragmenter. Observed: P95 latency down 18% on high-KV sessions (>2k entries); average GPU memory headroom increased by 12%; CPU overhead ~+3% of scheduler cycles. Microbenchmarks (local): fragment formation latency <200us per batch on 64 concurrent sessions. Notes: improvement concentrated on chat flows with many cached prefixes (system prompts + long histories).
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Fingerprint model misclassifies and causes over-fragmentation -> leads to throughput loss. Mitigation: conservative thresholds in canary, bounded fragment count per batch, and backpressure to legacy batcher. Risk: Pinning hot KV keys may starve other sessions -> mitigate via dynamic eviction window and per-customer fairness quotas.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature-flagged canary on dev-dedicated-3 (10% sessions) for 1 week. 2) Expand to 30% with observability gates (P95, OOM count, token throughput). 3) Full rollout to streaming-prod with staged ramp and automatic rollback on predefined thresholds. 4) Postmortem and tuning window.
